source: Grasshoff and May (2003) Krebs and Henseleit notebooks and the urea cycle, reconstructed with computer models (via MPIWG project page)
finding: Both complete notebooks (Krebs and Henseleit) survive. The Urea Modeler simulates the 1932 discovery step by step, first in PROLOG, later in Java. It was used to study experimental design, instrument set-up, error correction and the origin of hypotheses.
numbers: Project dates 2017-2023; discovery 1932; chapter pp. 269-294 in Reworking the Bench (Kluwer 2003). The page gives no quantitative results.
limits: Project page only; model internals and success measures not stated there. The chapter itself was not read.
agent_relevance: Shows a notebook can be turned into an executable operator sequence. Our log of operators and checks can be audited the same way.

source: Kulkarni and Simon (1988) The processes of scientific discovery: the strategy of experimentation (KEKADA)
finding: KEKADA is a production-system model of Krebs's 1932 urea work. It reacts to surprising results, builds explanations and plans next experiments, following what notebooks and interviews show.
numbers: No numbers read. Search snippet only; the CMU page returned 403.
limits: Not opened. Heuristic rules and the match to the notebook were not verified this session.
agent_relevance: Template for impasse handling: a surprise triggers a focused sub-search rather than a restart. Check against the full paper before use.
quote: reacts to surprises, formulates explanations, and carries out experiments

source: Holmes (1991, 1993) Hans Krebs: the formation of a scientific life; Architect of Intermediary Metabolism
finding: Holmes read Krebs's notebooks to follow his steps day by day. Not opened this session; listed only because SUBFIELDS.md names it as the founding study. Details belong to the other angles.
numbers: none verified
limits: Not opened; no claim made beyond its existence.
agent_relevance: Defines what 'real order of operators' evidence looks like. No machine claim.

source: Pavel Panchekha (blog) Can an LLM reproduce Kepler from raw data
finding: A single-author blog test of an LLM rediscovering Kepler from timestamped angular data in a clean setup. Seen as a search result only.
numbers: No results read.
limits: Not opened. Anecdotal, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: Candidate informal check of historical rediscovery. Do not cite for numbers.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld: a virtual environment for automated scientific discovery agents (NeurIPS D&B)
finding: 120 tasks, 8 topics, 3 difficulty levels. Baseline agents (ReAct, Plan+Execute, Hypothesizer) struggle; 11 human scientists do much better.
numbers: Best agent (ReAct) completed 38% of easy and 18% of challenge tasks. Hypothesizer found 34% of gold knowledge on easy and 8% on challenge tasks. Humans (N=11, MSc/PhD): average completion 66%, knowledge 55%.
limits: Text-based simulated world, three agent designs, GPT-4o era models. Humans played one seed once.
agent_relevance: Agents manage parts (unit-test tasks 60%+) but fail end to end. Our impasse detector must cover the whole cycle, not single steps.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld, Hypothesizer agent (appendix D.3)
finding: Hypothesizer keeps a running notebook: hypotheses with status (confirmed, rejected, pending) plus evidence, and measurements. Memory is updated after every action and summarised every 10 actions. It needs 2N LLM calls for N steps.
numbers: Memory cap 40 entries and 2k tokens; summarise every 10 actions; 2N calls per N steps.
limits: It scored best on knowledge but not on task completion (ReAct finished more tasks).
agent_relevance: A working LLM-agent notebook with explicit status per hypothesis. Close to our S9 look-back record; cost is double calls.

source: Majumder et al. (2024) DiscoveryBench: data-driven discovery with LLMs
finding: 264 real tasks from papers in 6 domains plus 903 synthetic tasks. Best system scores only about 25%.
numbers: Peak 25%. Biology 0%, engineering 7%, economics 25%, sociology 23%. Reflexion with oracle feedback beat plain CodeGen; ReAct-style prompts and a self-critic (DataVoyager) did not beat plain CodeGen.
limits: Facet-based scoring; GPT-4 class models.
agent_relevance: Added reasoning prompts did not help; real feedback did. Fits G2 (revise only from real output).
quote: even the best system scores only 25%

source: Majumder et al. (2024) DiscoveryBench, domain-knowledge hints
finding: DataVoyager (GPT-4o) scored 9.9% with domain knowledge versus 17.5% without it, as the paper's text reads.
numbers: 9.9% vs 17.5%. The sentence in the paper is phrased ambiguously, so verify direction before use.
limits: Single system, single comparison.
agent_relevance: Extra context can hurt. Test any notebook or hint injection at equal tokens (G7).

source: Chen et al. (2025) ScienceAgentBench (ICLR 2025)
finding: Data-driven discovery tasks from peer-reviewed papers. Execution feedback (self-debug) nearly doubles success for Claude-3.5-Sonnet.
numbers: Direct prompting 16.7% (20.6% with expert knowledge). Self-debug 32.4% (34.3% with knowledge), a 1.94x gain. o1-preview with self-debug reached 42.2%. Three attempts per task.
limits: Success needs program output to match; programs are often right in structure but wrong in details.
agent_relevance: Re-running with the real error output is the biggest lever here. Supports G2 and a look-back step that reads real failures.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist
finding: End-to-end idea, code, experiment, paper loop. The authors list their own failures: wrong implementations, hallucinated results, invented hardware facts.
numbers: Cost under 15 dollars per paper. An early version hallucinated entire results; ablation tables were sometimes invented.
limits: Self-report by the system's authors.
agent_relevance: A written run log is not proof. Results must come from code output (G2, G3).

source: Beel, Kan and Baumgart (2025) Evaluating Sakana's AI Scientist: bold claims, mixed results
finding: Independent re-run of the AI Scientist. Its novelty check is keyword search and labels known ideas (such as micro-batching for SGD) as novel. Many experiments fail or give logically flawed output.
numbers: 5 of 12 experiments (42%) failed from coding errors. Each code revision added only about 8% more characters. Median 5 citations per paper; 5 of 34 citations from 2020 or later. 4 of 7 manuscripts (57%) had structural errors.
limits: Small sample (12 ideas, 7 manuscripts), one domain (recommender-system ideas), one template.
agent_relevance: A critical replication of the headline claim. Fits G8: do not let the system judge its own novelty.

source: Yamada et al. (2025) The AI Scientist-v2: agentic tree search
finding: Replaces the linear loop with tree search over experiment nodes (draft, debug, improve, ablation). Failed nodes are marked buggy and the error is recorded for later debugging.
numbers: 3 manuscripts submitted to an ICLR workshop; one scored 6.33 (6, 6, 7) and passed; two were rejected. The accepted paper was withdrawn by design.
limits: N=3 papers, workshop level; acceptance is a weak measure.
agent_relevance: Every node keeps its own record and failed branches stay in memory. A notebook with branches, close to our S6 and S9.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SR: scientific equation discovery via programming with LLMs (ICLR 2025)
finding: Keeps a memory of earlier equations and fits constants with an optimiser. Ablations show which part matters.
numbers: Without iterative refinement NMSE is 1.01e-1 in-domain and 1.81e-1 out of domain. Without skeleton plus optimizer: 3.78e-1 and 3.75e-1. Removing the problem description also hurt considerably.
limits: Physics, biology and materials tasks; ablation numbers read from text, tables not re-checked.
agent_relevance: Feedback from fitting plus a memory of past tries beats one-shot sampling. Supports an operator log the next step reads.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench
finding: Benchmark built to resist memorisation. The best system solves only about a third by symbolic accuracy.
numbers: Best symbolic accuracy 31.5% on LSR-Transform and 28.1% on the other subset, as the text reads; out-of-domain test sets added.
limits: Full tables not checked here.
agent_relevance: Fitting data is not enough (G3): symbolic accuracy and out-of-domain fit are separate checks.

source: Zheng et al. (2026) NewtonBench: scientific law discovery in LLM agents (ICLR 2026)
finding: 324 counterfactual law-discovery tasks in 12 physics areas, 11 models. Ability is real but fragile: it falls with system complexity and with noise.
numbers: Noise of 0.0001 alone cuts symbolic accuracy 12-16% versus noise-free. A code tool helps weak models and slightly hurts strong ones (symbolic accuracy of 40% or more).
limits: Simulated systems.
agent_relevance: Fragility to noise argues for replicate checks before trusting a pattern.

source: Zheng et al. (2026) NewtonBench, code assistance paradox (section 4.5)
finding: A code interpreter makes strong models stop exploring early. The exploration-token rate (What if, Alternatively) falls as code budget rises, while exploitation tokens (Confirm, Verify) rise.
numbers: Performance falls when code budget goes from 0 to 1 for Gemini-2.5-flash and GPT-5-mini; weaker models improve.
limits: Only reasoning models with visible traces could be measured; four models.
agent_relevance: The early-exploitation trap our impasse detector must catch: cheap checking can end search too soon.

source: Zheng et al. (2026) NewtonBench, inference scaling (section 4.4)
finding: Reasoning models spend more tokens as tasks get harder; non-reasoning models do not, even with more rounds.
numbers: Qualitative curve; tokens per round rise with difficulty only for the Gemini-2.5 and GPT-5 families.
limits: Read from figure text.
agent_relevance: Effort should scale with difficulty; a counted budget with a difficulty signal fits this.

source: Geng, Chen, Arumugam and Griffiths (2025) Are LLMs reliable AI scientists? Reverse-engineering black boxes
finding: From observation alone, GPT-4o plateaus below the Bayesian ideal. Letting it intervene (query inputs it chooses) improves results.
numbers: Three black-box types (programs, formal languages, math equations), 3 seeds, GPT-4o; 10 initial observations then 5 to 50 intervention rounds. Gains by complexity level range from -0.6 to +12.7 descriptive-score points.
limits: Noise-free black boxes; GPT-4o as both reverse engineer and judge; LLM-judge score 0-10.
agent_relevance: Choosing the next test is where the gain comes from, not more data. Fits operator choice at S6.

source: Geng et al. (2025) reverse-engineering, failure modes
finding: Two failure modes: overcomplication (invents unneeded structure) and overlooking (ignores data). 20 failed cases per box were hand-labelled.
numbers: Program: 17 of 20 overcomplication. Math equation: 16 of 20 overlooking. Formal language: 8 overcomplication, 11 overlooking, 1 not applicable.
limits: 20 cases per box, human labels, one model.
agent_relevance: Two distinct stuck states with different fixes; the impasse detector could tell them apart.

source: Geng et al. (2025) reverse-engineering, yoked control
finding: Yoked design (borrowed from human learning studies): replaying the model's own intervention data to it helps less than doing the interventions. Doing the testing matters, not only the data.
numbers: Intervention-yoked below observation-intervention in all three box types. Llama-3.3-70B given GPT-4o's intervention data did about as well as or slightly better than observation-only, and below its own interventions.
limits: Plot-read values; no significance test reported.
agent_relevance: Notebook entries written by another model help less. Each run should read its own recorded operators and failures.

source: Geng et al. (2025) reverse-engineering, intervention strategies (Table 1)
finding: Reasoning once every five queries helps. Writing the box as Python code gave no extra gain.
numbers: Program: 43.4, 47.6, 19.2, 50.8 across four strategies (plain, descriptive, functional, analyze-then-query). Formal language: 24.1, 28.6, 22.8, 34.7. Math equation: 34.8, 38.8, 39.9, 38.0.
limits: One model, three seeds; column mapping read from flattened table text, so check before use.
agent_relevance: Periodic analysis (not every step) is a cheap trigger rule. Matches G1.

source: Chen et al. (2026) Auto-Discovery-Bench: structured state tracking in oracle-guided discovery
finding: Deterministic hidden-structure tasks. Accuracy falls with variables, trajectory length and distractors. Failures persist even when intervention choice and hypothesis writing are removed, so tracking the history is a bottleneck.
numbers: Relational graph with 10 houses: Grok-4 and Gemini-2.5-pro 100% success (10.4 and 10.1 average iterations); GPT-4o 30%; Qwen2.5 0%. Claude-3.5-haiku 20% to 0% and Llama 70% to 30% as size grows.
limits: Synthetic, noise-free; the authors say it does not replace realistic environments.
agent_relevance: Supports a program-kept record of past tries instead of relying on the model to recall them.

source: Wang et al. (2026) FIRE-Bench: rediscovery of scientific insights (ICML 2026)
finding: Agents must re-derive a published finding from only the research question. Strongest agents stay under 50 F1 with high run-to-run variance.
numbers: Claude Code (Sonnet-4) F1 46.7 (SD 23.4), Codex gpt-5-medium 41.9, OpenHands gpt-5 37.9, OpenHands o4-mini 31.9. 30 tasks; Claude Code best on 13, Codex 9, OpenHands 6. Backbone upgrade o4-mini to gpt-5: +6.1 F1 for +21% cost.
limits: Tasks are LLM-behaviour analysis papers; contamination check in the paper (gpt-5 fell 44.5 to 23.1 on a post-cutoff subset).
agent_relevance: Closest machine test of reconstructing a scientist's steps. Variance is huge: single runs prove little.

source: Wang et al. (2026) FIRE-Bench, error analysis
finding: Errors cluster in research planning (method deviation, goal deviation) and conclusion formation (unsupported or overgeneralised claims), across all four agents.
numbers: False positives: 76.4% to 95.0% are contradictory or unrelated; only 4.5% to 10.9% are plausible alternatives.
limits: LLM-assisted error labelling, human-verified; authors call the similarity of error profiles qualitative.
agent_relevance: Most wrong claims are not creative alternatives, so G2 and G3 checks catch them. Checking the final claim against the run log is the key control.

source: Safdar and Saadeldin (2026) Long-horizon autonomous architecture research with a language-model agent
finding: One agent, about 100 single-variable experiments, each recorded in a structured notebook (motivation, literature, change, budget, outcome). Productivity has three phases: rapid gain, a long saturation wall, then recovery.
numbers: Saturation regime: 29 hypotheses with near-zero gain. One early hypothesis (an FFN in channel-attention blocks) gave +21.41 points, 79.5% of the total CIFAR-10 gain. CIFAR-10 69.67% to 96.59%. Acceptance rate 36-38% in early phases versus 12% in Phase 3.
limits: Single run, single agent, single problem, no control arm; a human declared the phase changes.
agent_relevance: The machine counterpart of notebook study. The agent could not detect its own saturation from the log: the S6 impasse detector must be code, not model judgment.

source: Safdar and Saadeldin (2026) long-horizon agent, tool-access transition (Table 7)
finding: Literature access did not raise the size of the best gain but changed the kind of hypothesis. Code-changing hypotheses went from 5% to 76%; novel mechanisms from 2 to 8.
numbers: 2/42 = 5% code changes without literature tools; 16/21 = 76% with them. Novel mechanisms 2 vs 8.
limits: Confounded with phase and time; no randomised comparison.
agent_relevance: Escape from the impasse came from widening the action set, not from rethinking. Maps to adding operators by code on a signal.

source: Safdar and Saadeldin (2026) long-horizon agent, greedy anchoring
finding: The agent wrote 'pivot to a fundamentally different operator family' in its notes, then proposed another small change nearby on the next turn. The commit-or-discard rule makes the loop equal to greedy hill climbing.
numbers: Final stretch of Phase 3: +0.26 points over eighteen hypotheses with only two accepted.
limits: Qualitative reading by the authors, single run.
agent_relevance: Stated intent in notes is not behaviour. Escalation must be forced by a counter in code, not written as advice to the model.
quote: The instinct to escalate is present in the agent's verbal reasoning; the action consistently follows the gradient instead.

source: Practitioner notebooks for agents (osteele research-lab-notebook essay; SciLog)
finding: Blog posts and tools propose a structured notes file (hypothesis before run, measurement after) as agent memory. Seen in search results only.
numbers: No measured outcome data found.
limits: Not opened; opinion and tooling, not evaluation.
agent_relevance: Gap: no controlled study found that compares an agent with and without a lab-notebook log at equal tokens. A test we could run.

source: Agents of Discovery (2025) LHC Olympics anomaly detection with LLM agents
finding: A team of LLM agents runs an anomaly-detection analysis; prompting strategies and models are compared over repeated runs. GPT-5 was the most capable.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Search snippet only; a referee noted that a few high outliers pull the average up.
agent_relevance: Repeated-run variance reporting is the right practice. Do not treat averages with outliers as stable.

source: Search gap, 2020-2026: LLM studies replaying historical notebooks (Krebs, Darwin)
finding: Searches found no LLM study that replays Krebs, Darwin or other historical notebooks and scores operator order against the record. Computational reconstructions stop at KEKADA (1988) and the Urea Modeler (2003).
numbers: 0 studies found in a handful of searches; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex quotas were exhausted.
limits: Absence of evidence from limited search tools only.
agent_relevance: Open niche. We could build the test: give an LLM a Krebs notebook day by day and score its next-step choice against the real one.
